items.originalTitle: Trump’s War Poses a “Generational Threat” to Wildlife in the Persian Gulf
items.author: Lorenzo Tondo
items.title: Trump’s War Poses a “Generational Threat” to Wildlife in the Persian Gulf
items.summary: This story was originally published b y Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. The vast, dark slicks in the Strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Persian Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish. Eight months into the war between the United States and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the center of a growing environmental disaster . The naval blockade of the Strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture. The Strait, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life. It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development. Satellite view of a major fire at the Port of Salalah oil storage tanks in Oman after an Iranian drone strike on March 11, 2026. Gallo Images/Getty Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them. Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis. Added together, says a Greenpeace expert, the spills would cover “approximately 20,000 square kilometers—almost the size of Wales.” “Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said. “Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.” Since the war began on February 28, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed. “Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometers—almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief. More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November. Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles. A satellite image dated October 19 shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear.” Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 230 square miles at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organization Pax. An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick. Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites. Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta , two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves. Environmental organizations are continuing to analyze satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war. Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships. According to a Wall Street Journal report , the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island. In some instances, countries bordering the Strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on October 30 that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining. In Oman , divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands. An oil slick along the southern coast of Qeshm Island, Iran, ISNA / AFP / Getty But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said. Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds, and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the Strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.” Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems. A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar—the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down—on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea. Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface. “Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades—so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

items.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
items.summary: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

items.originalTitle: ChatGPT, Friendship Analyst
items.author: Illustration by Ananya Broker Parekh
items.title: ChatGPT, Friendship Analyst
items.summary: A few weeks ago, a chatbot read a tranche of my text messages spanning more than a dozen years and declared that I’d been a bad friend. First, some context: I’m writing a memoir about my love life, or lack thereof, so I’ve been going through old correspondence and quizzing friends about their memories of the years when I was single (2012–22) and not so single (2022–now). One of those friends is Michael—who, like me, is unmarried; who, like me, has an extensive history of encounters facilitated by dating apps; and who, like me, was long looking for love but often found himself disappointed. My text history with Michael goes back to 2014, when we first met. Sometimes, we’re in touch daily. At other times, we go weeks, months, even a year without communicating (for reasons that have never been entirely clear to us). Six years ago, I moved from New York, where Michael lives, to Los Angeles, so since then, our friendship has been conducted largely via phone. This means that an already rich history of friendship has become richer, not just because of the accumulation of our shared experiences, but also because of the way our communications have been automatically documented and archived. A text thread, when you think about it, is an incredible repository of primary source material—in effect, a data set—containing clues to how people conduct countless aspects of their lives, whether mundane or profound. For a memoirist, such material can be a gold mine. (I suspect that future historians will agree.) More freewheeling than, say, letters or emails, texts capture the immediacy of a writer’s feelings and observations and, because of that, can seem particularly “authentic.” [ Read: Archivists aren’t ready for the ‘very online’ era ] My initial quest for love-life insights within my archive with Michael yielded somewhat frustrating results. When I searched for words such as guy and date and sex , I quickly became overwhelmed and called him to complain: “There’s too much material for me to handle.” A few minutes later, my phone dinged. Michael had sent me an Excel spreadsheet containing our entire text history and suggested that I upload it into ChatGPT. I adored the idea. I’d been playing with chatbots for about a year and a half. For my memoir, I’d used them to pull out important strands from the transcripts of audio and Zoom interviews. I confess that I also once used a chatbot to give me an astrological analysis of a potential romantic relationship. So, with little hesitation, I took Michael’s advice, fed ChatGPT our data, and awaited the results. They weren’t all that surprising, at least when it came to the bot’s analysis of my romantic life. (Among other things, it told me that I had bad taste in men.) But I noticed that it shared some wholly unexpected stuff about my friendship with Michael (for instance: “Neither has to construct a respectable version of the self for the other”). Interesting , I thought. ChatGPT had expanded its feedback beyond an analysis of my love life to an analysis of the relationship framing the discussions of my love life. I wondered: If I asked it to go deeper on Michael and me, what more might it say? N ever before have we had the means to synthesize, so quickly, words poured unadulterated into a single device. A few years ago, one technologist imported into an app he created every WhatsApp message he’d ever sent or received, and had the algorithm analyze his interactions with people including his wife and father. As he told a New Yorker reporter, “A lot of people don’t realize that, essentially, their WhatsApp history—across all their chats—is the diary they didn’t know they’d been writing.” But conducting wide-scale analyses of entire relationships like this also has the potential to launch us into sticky ethical territory. Many people think of text messages as ephemeral and private (despite evidence of the various ways we can be easily surveilled). Our text threads with family and friends—the people we’re closest with—can therefore be quite honest, quite raw. “We had no idea when we started emailing and texting in the ’90s, 2000s, that these were records we’d be creating between us, which until that time were evanescent,” Jeff Hancock, a communication professor at Stanford University who studies AI-assisted conversation, told me. “Who knew that this would be a massive new thing,” he said, the fact that “private conversations between individuals would now have a record?” The idea that a person can so casually take the contents of their written communications—with or without other people’s consent—and ask an AI tool to ingest and analyze that data seems disquieting, if not downright dystopian. Hancock said that people’s use of chatbots to audit what we previously thought of as closed conversations will no doubt become more prevalent. This might feel like an intrusion, he acknowledged, but he could see net-positive benefits. Imagine a scenario, he suggested, in which “you’re like, Hey, look, I want to do right by my sister. I’ve been annoyed and frustrated with her .” A bot analyzing your text history might come up with the perfect thing to say the next time you call her. [ Read: The people who outsource emotional labor to AI ] Even so, Hancock noted that there are probably “lots of ways this will go wrong.” Consider chatbots that might not only analyze relationships as they evolve but also predict outcomes—which sounds a little Minority Report to me. And then there’s the question of accuracy: Chatbots are designed to serve, which means that they tend to communicate what they think people want to hear. Sometimes, an AI might “really unlock stuff” for a person, Hancock said. “But they’re sycophantic.” To be useful, the AI needs “to also take the perspective of the other person.” W hen I fed my text thread with Michael into ChatGPT, I found out—as I’d first hoped—a few things about my love life. I learned that I’m overly credulous when it comes to men’s stated intentions (“You can recognize that a man is unavailable, evasive, selfish, or inconsistent,” the bot said, “and nevertheless continue to treat his expressions of desire as evidence that something more meaningful might develop”) and that I’m looking for love in all the wrong places (“You sometimes recognize a man’s limitations but behave as though they are negotiable”). Yet when the bot pivoted to spicy comments about Michael and me, it really drew me in. It said, for instance, that I have selective hearing and can be dismissive after he has offered well-meaning advice: “You ask him what he would do, but instead of seriously entertaining his answer, you almost instantly construct the case against it.” So, with Michael’s permission, I came up with a new query and pressed harder: “Please analyze this data set of text messages between Michael Wertheim and Anna Holmes, two friends, and craft a portrait of their friendship over the years.” I asked ChatGPT to look not just at what he and I had said to each other but at how we’d said it. After three minutes and 53 seconds, it told me that it had analyzed the entire archive—32,245 messages, from September 13, 2014, to June 25, 2026. It had a lot to say. “Their language with each other is extraordinarily unguarded,” it told me. “They discuss work humiliation, money, parents, family dysfunction, depression and anxiety, illness, aging, sex, dating apps, hookups, rejection, medications, bodily problems, loneliness and death.” And: “They can move in seconds from something serious to something ridiculous, from mortality to television, from depression to a bad date, from career anxiety to cat litter.” And: “Their friendship eventually acquires some of the infrastructure of family.” When I told a friend about this experiment and read her a few lines, though, she made a smart observation: It sounded like ChatGPT was presenting a pretty rosy picture of my part in the friendship. What if, she asked, I pushed it for a more candid assessment? So I asked it to be more brutally honest. In response, it conceded that it had been “somewhat restrained” in its analysis—and proceeded to give me some real talk, telling me, in bold type, “There are moments where I think you are plainly the harder person to be friends with .” It also shared a rather damning 10-point list of my transgressions, including a paragraph or two of elaboration with each item. Among its observations: “You can disappear into your own life and assume the friendship will simply survive it.” “You can center your interpretation of his experience over his own.” “You can be relentless when you think Michael is handling something badly.” “You can be absorbed enough in your own distress that Michael has to announce his needs explicitly.” Ouch. It stung because I’ve always worried that this is true; the bot’s assessment felt like a confirmation of that fear. It seemed to be saying: You’re easily distracted, myopic, over-opinionated, selfish . If I wanted to give myself some grace, I could remind myself that even though ChatGPT had a corpus of communication between us, this was still merely a snapshot of the relationship, not a complete picture. Surely the AI was blind to bits of nuance and didn’t always understand context or intent. Yes, I can disappear into my own life and assume that the friendship will survive—but that’s the case with many close friendships. And yes, I can be “relentless,” but Michael has known from the beginning that I’m trenchant when giving advice because I assume that he wants honesty rather than enablement. (Though I probably need to ask him if that’s true.) ChatGPT also represents only one AI-generated opinion. As I was writing this article, Apple updated its Siri AI to go through iPhone users’ text messages and emails to propose next steps (such as adding a calendar event based on a conversation with a friend). I realized that a tool for real-time friendship analysis might now be built right into my phone. To test it, I asked Siri to examine my text history with Michael—and it was much kinder to me than ChatGPT, even when I asked it to be less sycophantic: I’m a reliable and supportive confidant, it said; if our relationship is asymmetrical, this is because it “appears to revolve more around his needs and schedule than yours.” What to make of this? Perhaps only that an AI’s analysis is subjective and possibly unreliable, kind of like the opinions of one’s real-life friends. Text messages aside, Michael and I communicate meaningfully in other ways—via voice calls, in person. Those interactions aren’t memorialized in a text thread, so they’re perhaps not as easy to analyze. But they offer something that a back-and-forth over a smartphone doesn’t, and that I’d argue can be just as revealing: tone, timbre, facial expressions, eye contact. Put another way, they offer feeling . After all of this AI analysis, I felt a mixture of fascination and unease. The insights that ChatGPT offered were more compelling than I’d suspected they would be, yet I’m hesitant to feed more of my texts to a bot. I’m conscious of the need for consent. And I’ve decided never to upload another person’s chats without permission, because the violation would be twofold: the downloading of the texts in the first place, and the analysis of them in the second. I also worry that gaps in a chatbot’s reading might lead me to wrongly or unfairly assess relationships that are important to me, or new and tender. Take the text thread between my boyfriend and me. Our communications over iMessage are fairly thin. I have no doubt that if a bot were to analyze our texts, it would characterize me as overly chatty and him as reticent and at times unresponsive. In real life, I know that if he’s unresponsive, this is typically because he’s at work . But on a day when I might be feeling less generous toward him, I could imagine recalling the AI’s analysis and becoming resentful—or constructing relationship-doomsday scenarios in my head. And what good would that do? As another friend of mine put it: I would only do this sort of analysis with someone I didn’t want to be friends with anymore . Chatbots may tell us a lot. But perhaps, as with astrology, we should consider their assessments of our most important relationships not as determinative but as opportunities to be more thoughtful—and we should see their advice less as an edict than as a nudge. I mean, all of us could probably be better to our loved ones. In the end, I don’t need a chatbot to tell me what I already know. items.originalTitle: This Comic Kills Technofascists
items.author: Dave Maass
items.title: This Comic Kills Technofascists
items.summary: Dave Maass has been writing about comics for more than 20 years, and now he also writes comics. By day, he teaches tech investigative techniques at the University of Nevada, Reno Reynolds School of Journalism and researches surveillance at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. If I was the manager of a comic book store, I’d create a section for “journalism nerdcore.” It’s where I would stock Transmetropolitan, DMZ, and Abbott – comics that place fictional journalists in the center of genre stories, be it science fiction, action or horror. Despite their daylight jobs, Spider-Man and Superman wouldn’t be allowed there, but DC’s Lois Lane would find a home of her own. On the end-of-shelf display, with a big fat, Sharpie-written “Employee Pick of 2026” sign: Exploit , the new comic series from Laura Hudson and Tim Leong and illustrator Emiliana Pinna, which was just published last month by Mad Cave Studios in its collected trade paperback volume . It doesn’t get more journalism nerdcore than its tag line: “Don’t Bury The Lede. Bury Your Enemies!” Exploit is an action thriller inspired by the battle raging right now between the tech oligarchy and the independent press. Editorial intern Kirby Kuo is trying to score her first byline in RIOT! , a WIRED -style print magazine, before the newsroom is wiped out by its soon-to-be new owner, a thin-skinned Alex Karp-flavored cyberlibertarian-turned-technofascist. But when the subject of her reporting is assassinated on a live stream, Kirby finds herself facing the blame, on the run and forced to place her trust in agoraphobic hacker Lenox and Cold War-alum cybermercenary Ipsum. Creators Hudson and Leong shared the masthead at WIRED (senior editor and director of digital design, respectively), but long before that they ran Comic Foundry , where they were “the team that changed comics journalism forever,” as ComicsBeat put it . Their careers have dovetailed between comics and journalism for years, with Hudson putting time at The Verge and ComicsAlliance and logging bylines in The Guardian, The New York Times, and Slate , and Leong holding creative roles at Fortune and Entertainment Weekly, while also writing and designing the Super Graphic series . All that experience shows. Between the chase sequences and heist-planning, there are plot points based on real episodes in tech and cybersecurity uncovered in publications like 404 Media, WIRED , and The Markup. But the panels radiate with the earnest love for scrappy, independent journalism–especially print journalism–and a molten fury for those who threaten it. I asked Hudson some questions to learn more about the heart and rage she poured into this series. The following has been edited for length and to avoid spoilers. Exploit explores the perils journalists face when handling leaked data. Dave Maass: Comics love an origin story. Take me through the back story of Exploit . Laura Hudson: We've been working on Exploit since we met up in a diner in LA in 2019, pre-pandemic. I don't live in LA but I was there working on a TV show, and it was the first time we'd lived in the same city since mid-aughts New York. Tim fucking LOVES print, and we'd both spent the last decade watching print journalism collapse from the inside. There are definitely scenes in the comic, and a few darlings we had to cut, that were ripped directly from real life whether anyone believes us or not. We arrived just after the good times had ended, in time to hear all the stories about how amazing it had been, and watch it get worse and worse. And of course, the generation just after us only experiences the wreckage. Tim had an idea for a comic set at a print magazine in New York, and I started imagining how I would feel, starting out as a journalist now. It always makes me think of donut blocks, from Super Mario Bros 3 on. They're the round, cakey-looking blocks in the game that start shaking when you step on them, and then fall down. So if you're going to walk across them, you better run, or you're gonna die. If you stop, you're gonna die. So, you can't stop. Ever. I understand that feeling intimately, and I knew I could write from there. And hell, I've wanted to make comics for over 30 years and now I'm finally doing it at 45? Fuck me. Exploit’ s main protagonist is a journalist (technically an intern) working for a magazine that specializes in tech investigations. It’s a WIRED meets Mother Jones kind of affair, but also if VICE’s Motherboard had been a standalone, hard-copy publication. Why choose a tech journalist as your hero? It probably says something about me that this question baffles me. Maybe I've just known too many good tech journalists, because to me it feels so obvious. Technology and the internet have played, are playing, and will play transformative roles in our lives, often in ways that few people fully understand. We're still governed by a gerontocracy where many of our leaders conceptualize the internet as a bewildering series of tubes, possibly now filled with AI. Our technology has surpassed our ability to legislate it or address it ethically to such an extreme degree that some tech leaders are actually asking to be stopped . The internet (or at least its infrastructure) is a hyperobject in the Mortonian sense of the word , something so massive, complex and distributed that people struggle to comprehend it fully. We can see pieces of it, and effects of it, but it's impossible to perceive or experience it as a whole, even and especially when we are inside it. But as Morton has written in reference to climate change, apocalyptic framing around hyperobjects can lead to hopelessness and inaction in situations when things genuinely can be addressed: "You are closing down the future. You are making your reader submit to tyrannical despair." Recognizing the enormity of something, in both the classic and popular sense, doesn't have to mean giving up. People who refuse to accept that something is too vast, too complicated, or too powerful to challenge are pretty compelling to me. That's what the best tech journalists do. Now let’s talk about the dual villains–both techbro executives at a start-up that is not only a government contractor, but aims to take over key government functions. Now the last comparable comic I read like this was 2014’s Hacktivist (written by of all people actor Alyssa Milano with Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly), and it also featured two very similar tech bros–but they were the heroes, moonlighting as digital freedom fighters. That was a time where people were inspired by larger-than-life figures like Jack Dorsey and Elon Musk. That's not so much the case anymore. How would you say that Exploit ’s antagonists reflect the shift in the public perception, and activities, of the “founder” class in our society? We want to believe that there is someone coming to save us, and since billionaires were the ones powerful enough to fuck up human civilization, it makes sense that we'd look for someone of equal power to save us. It makes sense to want that. But this is a fairytale we tell ourselves, which I say as someone who once wanted to believe it was at least possible. But no one is coming to save us. Let me say it one more time, because this is important: NO ONE IS COMING TO SAVE US. Billionaires least of all. Tech billionaires, by and large, are much better at destroying than fixing, and have advertised this fact for decades. They like to move fast and break things, and leave them broken. Many of them struggle to understand human beings socially even as they run social networks. They are prone to massive ego, can have anything they want at any time, and exist in bubble worlds where they are never told no. These are the people we're putting in charge of the future? I wouldn't put them in charge of a Dairy Queen. And I personally believe that some of them would be willing to accept the deaths of millions or even billions of people as the cost of advancing humanity in whatever sci-fi way they have imagined. Their obscene wealth requires them to exist at a scope that most humans are not built for, like images stretched out over miles. It distorts them as individuals, and it can distort their morality, insofar as it ever existed beyond the desire to advance and profit. This has become more evident as more tech leaders have chosen to behave as open buffoons in an age of buffoonery. But this is who they always were. In 2008, Exploit authors Laura Hudson and Tim Leong circa 2008 co-ran Comic Foundry. Courtesy: Laura Hudson From the first pages of the book, we’re introduced to the very real, extreme asymmetrical conflict between tech billionaires. Even a poorly paid journalist can threaten a billionaire (or at least his ego), but a billionaire has so much money, it’s easy to crush a publication. It immediately made me think of Jeff Bezos buying the Washington Post , Peter Thiel bankrolling the attacks on Gawker, and cases where surveillance companies have threatened news outlets. Am I wrong to think that’s the overarching theme of the whole series? Nope. I feel an anger about it so deep that I almost intuitively dissociate when it comes up. Not because I don't think I should be angry, but because I have learned I cannot be angry all the time without deleterious effects. Sometimes you just have to play the Yakety-Sax song in your head until the feeling passes, because you have to get things done today. It's worth noting that Kirby and Lenox (and Ipsum) [Note: Lenox is a young hacker and Ipsum is an old-school cybermercenary] undertake their mission with full knowledge that it will probably ruin their lives. That's part of the benefit package of being a billionaire. People can't challenge you without possibly ruining their lives. Now Exploit isn’t meant to be a realistic treatment of tech journalism, but I do think there’s a lot of truth in how you portray the perils faced by journalists who deal with hackers and leakers. This is running in a publication that specializes in that, but a lot of other journalists have been burned pretty bad, some even ending up in jail. How did reality affect the way you handled the relationship between your protagonist and the various hackers who enter her orbit? We've all seen things go very wrong for journalists, even those who meant well. Kirby has lived more life than the average intern, and done some journalistic work, but never at this level and never with these kinds of sources. She's green, and we wanted to show that. Before the big lead comes in, we have her pitching stories from sources that clearly have their own agenda, and her pitches get slapped down. That kind of pushback is essential, and what helps you learn before you're in a position to make serious mistakes. Kirby is pushed into a very big story before she is probably ready, but she's the only one in a position to do it. We wanted it to be clear that she's able to do what she does not just because she's smart and brave, but because she has an experienced group around her. Dealing with hackers, leakers, and sensitive sources requires dealing with two competing impulses as a journalist. Good journalism requires rigorous skepticism as a discipline. There's that journo saying that if your mother says she loves you, check it out. But developing a relationship with a source requires trust on both sides, and risk on both sides. One of the things Kirby learns is that a source is not necessarily an ally, even when they have valuable information. Their goals may overlap in places, but they can be different in invisible and dangerous ways. It's not something anyone should approach lightly or without care. A quarter of the way into the book, you introduce an assassination drone–and I initially expected it to be a sort of “Chekhov’s gun” that would play a huge role later on. But, it actually wasn’t. It turned out the most frightening thing still is people –specifically the mobs of doxxers who worship tech demagogues. Does this mirror your own experiences with online harassment? One of the things people used to say a lot, to dismiss or ignore the nightmarish world of online harassment, is that it was "only" online. You could just close your computer and go outside, so really, wasn't it all in your head? This line of convenient fiction collapsed pretty quickly, as doxxing, swatting, stalking, assaulting, raping, and molesting people through the internet became, shall we say, super popular? You can't dismiss the internet as a fake, unreal place where nothing of consequence matters. We know it matters now, that it's dangerous. But now it almost feels too late to care. These systems and the people who run them have certainly shown they don't care, and there's no Band-Aid you can put on it now to fix it. We could have built the internet and its social architecture very differently, in a way that prioritized dialogue over the right to abuse. But the trolls thought it was funny, and the companies wanted more money, so here we are living in the cursed labyrinth of their lols. One thing about an assassination drone, though: everyone understands it as a weapon. A tool of sorts, but one designed explicitly to cause damage. Its goals and impacts are not opaque. Social media platforms were pitched as a way to connect people, to give them the power to reach out and touch anyone from anywhere. Giving this power away to anyone who wanted it with little to no accountability was described by tech companies at the time as inherently good. It took longer—some would say too long—for everyone to realize the scope of the damage it could cause. Or that this incredible communications technology could double as a custom-made playground for grifters, bullies and predators of every stripe. So yeah, people are the scary part. But people get a lot scarier when they are given great power with zero accountability. RIOT magazine’s editor still has fucks left to give about investigative reporting. Zines play a major plot point in the book. But you also made a promotional zine for San Diego Comic-Con, which included a lot of digital security advice. How do you see physical media reemerging in political life? Tim designed that, by the way, and I can't believe how much it looks like an actual riot grrrl zine. Zines have long been linked to comics culture, and you can see the overlap in a lot of indie comics spaces and events. But zines—or as they once called them, pamphlets—have been powerful political tools for over 500 years. They have defeated churches and kings. And they're a very compelling tool right now, as a form of dissent that exists outside of the internet and its platforms. You can't hack a printed page. And we don't think about it this way anymore, but writing on paper is a communications technology—perhaps the greatest in the history of the world—and we should regard it as such. A lot of obsolete or antiquated tech can have value today because accessibility is also vulnerability, and obsolescence is its own kind of security feature. There are some impressive Gen Z zine enthusiasts, and a great WIRED article about the scene. But I'd love to see more people pick up that torch, for both creative and political reasons. No one can stop you. What do you hope people will take away from Exploit? How do you hope it will make them feel? In the year of our Lord 2026, I would be happy just to give people a bit of distraction from the horrors. But if you feel like your life has been suffused by the feeling that you showed up after the party was over, and that it's only downhill from here, then we made this, in part, for you. It's a grim feeling we know well, a sort of miasmic dread that flattens the future and makes you feel helpless and paralyzed. And that's exactly how a lot of terrible people want you to feel. They want you to lie down and allow the terrible machine to function smoothly around you. Both Kirby and Lenox come up with their own imperfect coping mechanisms for that reality and feeling, but they do cope. They do move forward and fight, and they don't do it alone. They can't, and neither can we.

items.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
items.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford declared Saturday that "the worst is behind us" after the U.S. saw its longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years this weekend. Transportation Sec. Sean Duffy says the situation arose when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing old copper wiring in the air traffic control system with new fiber wiring, causing a system overload. FAA UNVEILS NEW AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLER HIRING PLAN AFTER CHIEF WARNED SYSTEM WAS ‘CHRONICALLY UNDERSTAFFED’ The work led to "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours. Officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause," he said. "Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said. EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP'S FAA TOUTS NEW AI-POWERED TOOL HELPING THOUSANDS OF PASSENGERS AVOID FLIGHT DELAYS The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023 , when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. The FAA issued the ground stop order on Friday afternoon. UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE The ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, but the ripple effect felt by airline crews and passengers lasted with residual delays continuing to affect airport operations, ultimately impacting some 15,000 flights Friday and Saturday. "You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most," Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a post on X this weekend. items.originalTitle: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it
items.author: Geoff Woods
items.title: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it
items.summary: “Raise your hand if your executive team has mandated the use of AI.” I was standing on stage at the annual Great Places to Work convention in Las Vegas, and every one of the 500 CHROs I was in front of put their hands up. These were all HR leaders in mid-market and enterprise companies. “Now, keep your hands up if every single person on your executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable.” Almost every hand went down. I ask this question at every speaking engagement, and I’ve seen a pattern–and a problem. Company leaders are mandating the use of AI. With that mandate, they’re expecting increases in the productivity of their workforce. But they’re not holding themselves to the same standard. Executives often think that “leading AI” in their organizations means delegating the adoption and strategy of it to IT, a Chief AI Officer, or an outside consultant. That’s not delegation–that’s abdication. CEOs and executive teams need to learn to use AI, and become AI-driven leaders, before they can build AI-driven organizations. I say this as I’m starting to see companies increasingly tying AI goals and skills directly to employee raises and promotions. Should compensation be tied to AI skill? It depends on the company. If you’re an organization that typically ties performance to specific skills that will grow in value, it makes sense. If you don’t, it’s a break from precedent–but it doesn’t mean it’s the wrong move. What does concern me is when a CEO who doesn’t use AI is the one making the call. And by “use AI,” I don’t mean to help them write better emails–I mean truly leveraging it to think strategically and make themselves more valuable. Without that experience, a leader will limit their vision for what AI can actually do for their organization. It’s tough to describe color when you’ve only seen black and white. From search engine to thought partner The first time I saw AI, it was December 2022. I was the Chief Growth Officer at Jindal Steel, and ChatGPT had been out for about two weeks. When I saw AI, I saw the future. And like most leaders, I said to myself, “I’m really busy. I’ll revisit this later.” Like any good executive, I then thought about delegation. “I have a huge IT department,” I thought. “I’ll delegate this to them. Or maybe we will hire a consulting company to do it for us.” Then I remembered a quote from my college mentor: “Focus on mastering the skills that are so valuable, they’ll serve you no matter where you go.” At that moment, I knew AI would be one of those skills. That cemented my thinking. I needed to learn more about this myself, not delegate it. I started with a simple commitment. Use AI once a day, every day. Very quickly, I realized I was using it for things that really didn’t matter, like writing better emails. Last time I checked, I never received a promotion for the quality of my emails. I had this realization that I was using AI to major in the minors. Then I started to wonder, what would it look like to major in the majors? I started thinking about the skills I had that truly enabled me to deliver the most value. One of them was the ability to ask leaders the right strategic questions to unlock new levels of growth. In that moment, I realized I was asking AI questions like it was Google. I wondered what it would look like if I had AI ask me questions instead as a thought partner to elevate how I think and shift how I lead. That was the game changer. I started using AI to elevate how I think, which shifted how I was leading within Jindal Steel. A few months into my AI use, I was talking with Naveen Jindal, the Chairman of Jindal Steel. I told him how I was using AI for strategy instead of tactics, and he asked to see an example. I opened up my AI tool using the CRIT framework I’d developed, which stands for “Context,” “Role,” “Interview,” and “Task.” CONTEXT Attached is our annual strategic plan. (Which I attached into a secure instance of ChatGPT). ROLE Your role is to act as an aggressive, growth-minded board member with deep expertise in the steel industry, vertically integrated from distribution to mining. INTERVIEW Interview me. Ask me one question at a time, up to five questions, to understand where our plan may be insufficient to deliver results to the market. TASK Tell me where our plan may be insufficient to deliver the expected results and the actions we can take over the next 30 days to deliver on our next earnings call. AI started asking one sharp question at a time. Questions that only someone who knew our industry would ask. It pulled out all of the context that was in our heads. Then it laid out a real analysis of where the plan could break. Naveen’s mind was blown. “This is incredible,” he said. I agreed and suggested we should drive it through the whole company and that he should lead it as Chairman. His words? “I disagree. You do it!” The problem was, I knew almost nothing about AI. But I knew the power of asking the right questions. I asked, “Who could I get into a relationship with that could enable me to drive this across our company?” That led to a partnership with Google, where I learned a lot about the tech–and the more I learned about it, the less I realized how much the tech mattered. You can have the greatest technology in the world, but if you don’t win the hearts and minds of your people to harness the technology, you’ll never unlock the value. It became clear that AI adoption was about leadership. Over my time at Jindal, the market cap grew from $750 million to $12 billion over a four year period. This was done with the right strategic thinking—thinking that AI directly supported throughout the company. That is not about AI. It’s about the right strategic thinking. AI became supportive of that I went all-in on the leadership aspect of AI, to the point where I resigned from Jindal Steel, wrote a book about what I learned, and turned it into a company. Start with your biggest problem One of the questions I get asked often is, “If a CEO wanted to start this week, what’s the first piece of their own work they should test with AI?” Start by asking yourself something you’re already asking anyway: “What’s the biggest problem facing our company–the one that would unlock huge growth if you solved it?” That question gets you focused on the 20% of work that drives 80% of your results. Then, ask how AI can help. Write a prompt using CRIT: Describe the context in detail, tell AI what kind of expert you wish could advise you, have it interview you one question at a time, and give it a task, like, “Give me the top three high-impact, non-obvious strategies I could deploy to solve this problem.” Here’s the biggest piece of advice: Don’t take the AI response at face value. Tell AI what you like, don’t like, and would change about the response, and keep iterating on it until you’re confident enough to act. Inspect what you expect When you’re using AI as a thought partner, it becomes much easier to judge whether your people are using it in a way that improves how they think and moves the business forward. Most companies are measuring AI adoption through usage metrics (i.e. “80% of our workforce is using AI every week”). That’s a good place to start, but it doesn’t tell you whether people are actually using AI for high-value work. If you look closer, you’ll probably find that most of that usage is small tasks that don’t make anyone valuable to the company. The better test is to inspect what you expect. When your team walks you through how they solved a problem, ask how they used AI as part of the process. The ones who have bought into AI as a thought partner will be able to tell how it sharpened their thinking, or helped them see blind spots they would have missed. If all they can describe is time saved on emails and summarizing meeting notes, they’re complying with your adoption mandate, but haven’t really seen what AI can do for them. You can only coach people if you’ve done the work–and the learning–yourself. Rethink what you’re rewarding If your company has already tied compensation or raises to AI, take another look at what you’re measuring. If it’s just usage, you’re not tracking the skill that matters. The AI skills worth rewarding are the ones that will keep growing in value: the strategic thinking, or the great line of questioning. And if you’re a leader, be honest about whether your own pay is being held to the same standard as everyone else’s. The next time I ask the question about whether an executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable, I’m looking for every hand to stay up. items.originalTitle: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads
items.author: Preston Fore
items.title: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads
items.summary: Public universities helped make American higher education a draw for students and researchers worldwide. Now lawmakers and governing boards from Kansas to Utah want proof that the professors who teach there work hard enough. Faculty say the premise is backward. Professors who spoke with Fortune describe 55-hour weeks, departments that have shrunk by as much as half, and raises that haven’t kept pace with inflation. “We are losing ground,” said Renita Coleman , a journalism professor at the University of Texas at Austin. As scrutiny of higher education grows , state legislators, governing boards, and administrators have started questioning how professors spend their time and whether they deliver enough for their salaries and job protections. Some have pushed to limit tenure . Others are demanding a detailed accounting of faculty responsibilities. Critics see tenure as a shield for underperformers. Faculty say that misreads the job Public confidence in American higher education has fallen sharply over the past decade. According to Gallup , 38% of Americans expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education in 2026, down from 57% in 2015. The share expressing very little or no confidence rose from 10% to 25%. The weakening trust comes amid a convergence of concerns, from rising college costs and questions about the value of degrees to political battles on campuses . Those frustrations have fueled skepticism of tenure, which grants professors permanent faculty status after they meet a university’s standards for teaching, research, and service. Tenure was designed to safeguard academic freedom. But the American Council of Trustees and Alumni acknowledged in July that the public increasingly sees it as “a mere promise of job security, even for incompetent or unproductive professors.” Against that backdrop, lawmakers and university governing boards in states including Wisconsin , Utah , Ohio , and Kansas have moved to tighten faculty accountability. They have imposed minimum teaching loads, more rigorous post-tenure reviews, and other requirements to ensure professors do their share. For Coleman, the assumption that professors ease up once they earn tenure couldn’t be further from reality. “If they would only follow us around for a while, they would see this is ridiculous,” she said. “The pressure, the way they think, as soon as we get tenure, you’re going to stop working.” Earning tenure can take half a dozen years, and by then the pace of the job is habit. The idea of slowing down can feel almost foreign, Coleman said. “By the time we get tenure, we’re so ingrained in this, we can’t stop,” she said. George Dehner , a history professor and department chair at Wichita State University, said the scrutiny often starts from a basic disconnect about what professors do. “If you think the faculty are scamming you and don’t really work hard…this idea that faculty are working four or six hours a week teaching classes is a deep misunderstanding of what faculty do,” Dehner said. He and his peers “easily” work 55-hour weeks, he added, though their contracts stipulate 40-hour weeks during the nine-month academic year. Kansas now requires written work plans and five-year reviews for tenured faculty Many universities have long used a rough 40-40-20 model for faculty time: 40% teaching, 40% research, and 20% service to the institution and broader community. In January, the Kansas Board of Regents, which governs the state’s six public universities, put those expectations in writing. Under its new policy , faculty at the three research universities (the University of Kansas, Kansas State, and Wichita State) must devote 40% to 55% of their workload to teaching, 35% to 45% to research, and 5% to 20% to public service. At the three regional universities, teaching rises to 60% to 75%. Every faculty member now needs a written work plan, and annual reviews are mandatory. Those who fall short of workload expectations are placed on an improvement plan, and tenured faculty with two consecutive unsatisfactory annual reviews face dismissal, reassignment, or an additional one-year improvement plan. Tenured faculty will also undergo a comprehensive peer review every five years, down from every seven. Dehner described the policy as a concession to lawmakers who had pushed to give the regents greater authority to revoke tenure . Rather than protecting faculty, he argued, the new requirements reflect the same suspicion that professors aren’t doing enough. “It is absolutely not welcome,” Dehner said. “It comes from a space where there’s a deep suspicion that faculty don’t do anything… that’s a bad-faith place to start. This belief that faculty are lazy and are scamming them [is] compounded by the fact that they have no idea what higher education people do.” Gamal Weheba , an engineering professor at Wichita State, also sees the policy as an attempt to appease legislators rather than a meaningful measure of productivity. Academic work, he argued, can’t be measured by hours spent in a classroom or an office. “It’s not just an idea of having a time card that I clock in and clock out before I talk to students,” Weheba said. “That can never happen.” The Kansas Board of Regents did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. At a January meeting, Regent Matt Crocker said the new policies strengthen accountability for state higher education spending, the University Daily Kansan reported . “The question I seem to get all the time, especially being here in Topeka, is making sure I’m being a good steward for the state’s funding for higher education, and I think the program and policies help answer that question,” Crocker said. More work to go around, and fewer tenured professors to do it For faculty, one of the biggest frustrations with the new mandates is that they’re being asked to do more without more colleagues to share the load. When Coleman started teaching at UT Austin in 2005, her department had roughly 25 full-time tenured faculty members. Today it has about 18, a decline of roughly 28%. The same pattern shows up in Kansas. Dehner said Wichita State’s history department has shrunk from about 17 faculty members when he joined in 2004 to roughly nine today. In Weheba’s engineering department, the count has fallen from about 14 to eight. Nationally, about 32% of faculty members held full-time tenured or tenure-track appointments in fall 2023, down from about 53% in 1987, according to data from the American Association of University Professors (AAUP). The shrinking ranks matter because tenured faculty carry duties well beyond the classroom. They serve on university committees, advise students, help colleagues pursue research funding, and sit on search committees for new university leaders, a particularly time-consuming job amid the revolving door of college presidents . Professors also face problems that were far less prominent when many of them started: student mental health crises, the rapid adoption of AI, cuts to research funding, and political and social unrest on campus. “There are more burdens than ever being placed on faculty shoulders, which is putting incredible strain on them individually, but also strain on the overall ecosystem in higher ed,” said Geoff Watson, CEO of NCFDD , which provides faculty development resources. “When you put all of that together, more is being asked of faculty, and actually they’re being provided less support than they ever have been,” he added. None of that means professors should get a pass, or that they’re all complaining, Coleman said. Universities have long had ways to deal with faculty who don’t meet expectations, she noted, including pushing some out. A legislative audit released in Utah in October suggests those mechanisms don’t always work. Auditors examined materials from 666 performance reviews of tenured faculty, and only eight concluded that a professor’s teaching needed improvement. The auditors highlighted 40 cases in which professors received “satisfactory” ratings despite evidence of poor teaching. Utah Legislative Auditor General Kade Minchey told Fortune his office has also received allegations of harassment and of professors not showing up to class. The report pinned much of the problem on leadership. Department chairs, who are often responsible for holding faculty accountable, typically rotate through the job and take on its administrative duties on top of their own teaching, research, and service, leaving them little time or incentive to confront colleagues. “When chairs are faculty first and supervisors second, they may neglect the harder, time-intensive leadership responsibilities that drive accountability,” the report stated. The audit called on universities to strengthen the supervisory role of department leaders and redefine what chairs do. It also asked the Legislature to consider whether the minimum due process required to remove a tenured professor is excessive. Minchey stressed that the findings weren’t “an attack on tenure,” but rather “a problem of leadership, and it’s a problem of structure.” The strain on faculty isn’t a red-state or blue-state issue Much of the push for faculty accountability has come from Republican-led legislatures, and the Nov. 3 midterms reshuffled that map. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott . In Wisconsin, which wrote a minimum teaching load into law, Democrats flipped both legislative chambers . That gives some faculty reason for optimism, but neither result rewrites existing policy, and meaningful change is unlikely to happen overnight. The workload strain, meanwhile, isn’t confined to red states. In Massachusetts, free community college has helped drive enrollment up more than 43% since 2022, adding roughly 27,000 students, according to the state. The program has opened doors for students and added pressure on the professors who teach them. Darren Stocker , a criminal justice professor at Cape Cod Community College, typically teaches five classes a semester. Each can have as many as 32 students, and he often makes room for more. The result is workdays that stretch at least 12 hours, “from sun up to sundown, seven days a week,” he said, as he grades assignments, meets with students, prepares lectures, and handles his other responsibilities. Pay compounds the long hours. Stocker said Cape Cod housing costs have made it increasingly hard for educators to live near campus. “It’s very difficult to really live in the area in which you work,” Stocker said. “That’s the reality of it.” Average pay for full-time faculty rose 2.3% between fall 2024 and fall 2025, but inflation ran 2.7% over the same period, according to the AAUP’s annual report on faculty pay . Adjusted for inflation, faculty salaries remain 9.5% below their fall 2019 levels. Policy changes could ease some of that pressure. Rebuilding confidence in higher education, and the research capacity it has lost, will take considerably longer. “There is no more pressing issue for higher education than getting very serious about how we rebuild what’s been lost and hopefully build upon it from there,” Watson said. “But it’s not a short-fuse fix that is going to have to take years to kind of come back.” Stocker, for one, isn’t looking for a way out. “I absolutely love my job. I don’t think there’s anything I would ever want to do more than what I do now, and that’s teaching in the classroom,” Stocker said. “I live to see the success of my students.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: Inside Senate GOP's tense post-election reckoning as Thune clashes with Republican critics
items.title: Inside Senate GOP's tense post-election reckoning as Thune clashes with Republican critics
items.summary: Senate Republicans huddled for hours on end to define their remaining time in power and determine if the leadership they had backed so far was the right choice moving forward into a new era in Washington, D.C. Some closed-door meetings over the last nearly two years Republicans have controlled the Senate have been animated, with policy pitches devolving into shouting matches — President Donald Trump and Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., infamously sparred over the Iran war earlier this year. This confab, their first since Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats roared back into the majority, was different. In part, it was meant to develop a plan that would carry them through the final weeks of this year — that was agreed upon during the meeting, but not without its own drama after the fact on who could lay claim to the GOP’s 54-day blitz. SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE It was also a test to see if Republicans wanted to keep Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., as their leader, or delay until a challenger appeared. But Republicans pushing for a delay acknowledged part of the problem: Who would want the job? "I got the job because nobody else wants it," Thune told Fox News Digital after the dust settled in the Old Senate Chamber. And he did, along with much of the same leadership team that Senate Republicans elected when they won the majority two years ago, by acclamation, meaning no lawmaker objected to their leadership slate. Some told Fox News Digital it was like "Festivus," the holiday etched into Gen-Xers' brains from "Seinfeld" known for its airing of grievances. Others described it as a frank, needed debrief as the GOP picks through the debris of Election Night. GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS "It really was, to be honest with you, as profound as the loss was last week. I would have expected more emotions, which I consider to be a good sign," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital. "But I think it's almost — It's self-governing because nobody can dispute that it's a problem." "Now it's not like you're looking for the silver lining," he continued. "It doesn't exist. It is what it is, and you've got to react." But there were some "testy" moments, particularly between Thune and Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., the driving force behind the push to delay leadership elections. For Thune, the main question was what anyone else in the Senate GOP would have done differently in his shoes. "I just think that you come through an election like this and everybody's looking for scapegoats and there's a lot of blame casting that goes on, and I just wanted to get up and basically defend what we had done and accomplished," Thune said. "And I think the operative question is, tell me what you would do differently? Both on the political side and the legislative side. So we had a good, we had a robust conversation, and it does. It always gets a little bit testy in the back and forth, but I thought that, by and large, the discussion was very candid, and certainly gave everybody an opportunity to be heard." CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—' Johnson acknowledged that he was "prone to interrupting, I’m rude that way," and told Fox News Digital that he was sure Thune was "not happy that I did that," but assured that there was no "animus" between the two. "In politics, everything has to be so black and white, and, unfortunately, for our base, the way to really rev them up is inter-conference fighting, which is not helpful," Johnson said. "So, again, I didn't really like doing this, but it had to be done," he continued. "I mean, we had to, and in the end, I think, resulted in a very, very good conversation and pretty well revealed we're just lucky to have anybody who wants those jobs." Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital that Thune showed "moments of exceptional leadership" in the heat of the meeting. He noted that the top Republican's rebuttal reminded lawmakers of the "ebb and flow of the politics in our country," dating back to 1986, when former President Ronald Reagan, then entering his final midterm election similar to Trump, lost eight seats in the upper chamber. "Obama lost nine Senate seats in 2014, it looks like we're going to lose eight, depending on what happens in Alaska," Daines said. "So it's within the kind of the historic norms of going back and forth." "And the leader forcefully laid that out and then talked about what he needed to do going forward to unify and eventually reclaim the majority," he continued.
